readerTitle: Your team's new service needs a price by Friday
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (대형 상업 청소 회사 안의 신규 사업팀이 B2B 실내 공기질 관리 서비스를 출시) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 출시 가격은 숫자 하나가 아니라 세 가지 결정이다. 바닥(원가)과 천장(고객의 차선책) 사이에서 어디서 시작할지, 경쟁이 붙었을 때 어디를 지킬지를 정하는 일이다.
misconception: 신제품 가격은 원가에 마진을 붙이거나 경쟁사 가격에 맞추면 된다. 경쟁사가 내리면 따라 내려야 한다.

sources.text: 가격 전략의 표준 개념 (가치 기반 가격, 원가 가산, 경쟁 기반, 스키밍, 침투, 프리미엄 가격)
모든 수치와 상황은 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 원가 가산: $180 × 1.4 = $252. 고객의 차선책: 필터 교체 $300 + 분기 공기질 점검 $1,500 ÷ 3 = 월 $500, 합계 월 $800.
소프트웨어 노트의 '추가 사용자 비용이 거의 0에 가깝다'는 일반적 경향으로만 서술했습니다. 서버·지원 비용이 큰 제품은 예외일 수 있습니다.

cards.title: Your team's new service needs a price by Friday
body: You lead a three-person team inside a commercial cleaning company. Your new service is ready: air-quality sensors in client offices, plus monthly filter changes.
The launch deck is finished except for one slide. The price. Three people already have strong opinions about it.

image.label: A launch slide with a blank price box
image.brief: 회의실 화면에 출시 발표 슬라이드가 떠 있고, 가격 칸만 비어 있음 ("$___ / site / month"). 테이블 위에 작은 공기질 센서와 필터. 사람 세 명이 각자 다른 숫자가 적힌 포스트잇을 들고 있음. 실제 기업 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: The numbers on your desk.
body: Finance wants cost plus 40%. Sales wants to match the rival. Five facility managers you interviewed told you what they pay today.

breakdown.label: Your cost per site
breakdown.detail: Technician time, filters, sensor lease, per month

breakdown.label: Rival's price
breakdown.detail: An HVAC firm. Filter changes only, no monitoring

breakdown.label: Client's next-best option
breakdown.detail: $300 for filters plus a $1,500 quarterly air audit

cards.title: Where do you start the price?
body: You need one monthly price per site. Which number do you build from?

options.feedback: Easy to defend inside the company, but it puts you below a rival that does less. You leave most of the $800 value with the client and signal "budget option."
It feels safe, but the rival sells only filters. Matching its price tells clients your monitoring is worth nothing extra.

options.text: Start from the $800 alternative and price below it
options.feedback: Clients save money versus what they buy today, and you keep a healthy share of the value you create. Cost becomes your floor, not your price.

cards.title: Say you started from value.
body: You settle on about $550 as the long-run price. Then the parent company's sales team sends you 120 interested clients. You can serve only 40 this year.

options.text: Intro price of $299 to sign as many as possible
options.feedback: You fill 40 scarce slots at $119 a month each instead of $370, and turn away buyers who'd pay more. Raising the price later will feel like a broken promise.

options.text: Launch at $650 for the most demanding offices, then step down as you add technicians
options.feedback: Scarce capacity goes to the clients who value it most, at $470 a month each. Plan the price steps in advance so later cuts look like a schedule, not panic.

options.text: Charge $550 to everyone from day one
options.feedback: Simple and fair-looking. But with three buyers for every slot, whoever signs first gets a bargain they'd have paid more for.

cards.title: Say you launched at $650.
body: All 40 slots fill. Six months later, the HVAC rival adds a basic sensor and drops to $350. Two clients forward you its flyer.

options.feedback: Your margin per site falls from $470 to $170, and the rival can cut again. You've started a price war on its terms.

options.text: Hold at $650 and show the difference: monthly reports, same-day response, one vendor with cleaning
options.feedback: If the difference is real, the clients who chose you for it stay, and your margin stays. You may lose a few price-shoppers, and that's an acceptable cost.

options.text: Add a $350 filters-only plan next to the full service
options.feedback: It could catch price-shoppers. But some $650 clients may trade down, and you're now competing on the rival's ground.

cards.title: Every launch price sits between a floor and a ceiling.
body: Your cost is the **floor**: below it, every sale loses money. The customer's next-best option is the **ceiling**: above it, they'd rather keep what they have. Competitor prices show where customers will compare you.
Timing decides where you start in that range. Scarce capacity and eager buyers point high. A race for share, or a product that gets better with more users, points low.

image.label: A price band from $180 floor to $800 ceiling
image.brief: 가로 막대 하나. 왼쪽 끝 "Floor: your cost $180", 오른쪽 끝 "Ceiling: client's next-best option $800". 중간에 "Rival $300" 작은 표시, "Launch $650"과 "Long-run $550" 화살표. 바닥과 천장 사이 구간을 강조.

cards.softwareNote: In software the floor is often close to zero, since one more user costs little. That makes cost-plus almost useless and puts the weight on value and on the alternatives customers compare you with.

cards.title: High launch prices have conditions.
body: Starting high works when early buyers truly value it most and rivals can't copy quickly. Tell early clients up front that prices will change, or a later cut feels like a betrayal.
Holding a premium works only if the difference is real and visible to the buyer. If the rival's reports match yours next year, your $650 becomes a gap to explain, not a reason to pay.

cards.title: A launch price is three decisions, not one.
body: Here's how your calls map to this unit:
list: **Decision 1 → Value-based pricing.** Start from the customer's next-best option. Cost-plus and competitor prices are guardrails, not answers.
**Decision 2 → Price skimming vs penetration.** Scarce capacity and eager buyers favor starting high and stepping down.
**Decision 3 → Premium pricing.** Hold the price when the difference is real, and show it.
cards.callout: **Try it today:** for one product, write down its floor (your cost), its ceiling (the customer's next-best option) and where your price sits between them.
